segs.text: Module eight, objective one. Linear versus nonlinear pharmacokinetics. In linear pharmacokinetics the parameters, such as the half life and the clearance, do not change when different or multiple doses of a drug are given. In nonlinear pharmacokinetics, increased doses or chronic administration cause deviations from the profile seen with single doses, and the half life and the clearance change. She said, Linear, our parameters don't change, nonlinear, they do. Phenytoin is the prototype nonlinear drug in this course.

card.m: linear: t<sub>½</sub>, Cl unchanged with dose
nonlinear: higher or repeated doses → t<sub>½</sub>, Cl change
Ex. phenytoin

segs.text: Most drugs are eliminated by a first order process, which is linear. The amount removed per unit of time is proportional to the amount present, so the fraction removed per unit of time stays the same at every level. That is why the half life and the clearance are the same at every dose. So twice the dose gives twice the level at every time and twice the A U C, the area under the curve of level against time, and a first dose can be carried forward to steady state by superposition.

card.m: first order: amount removed per time ∝ amount present; fraction per time constant
→ t<sub>½</sub>, Cl the same at every dose
2 × dose → 2 × level, 2 × AUC (AUC ∝ dose); superposition

segs.text: Nonlinear pharmacokinetics comes from saturation of an enzyme or carrier system that can only work so fast. V max, the fastest elimination rate it can reach, is a rate: an amount or concentration per unit of time. K M is the concentration at which the rate is half of V max, and the drug level, C p, is low or high only compared with K M. Well below K M, the rate is a small part of V max, so the enzymes have spare capacity, and twice the level gives about twice the rate: first order. Well above K M, the enzymes are saturated: more drug raises the rate only a little, so it stays near V max: zero order. She said, That's as fast as it can go.

card.m: cause: a saturable enzyme or carrier
V<sub>max</sub>: the fastest elimination rate, a rate (her example 12 mg/kg/day)
K<sub>M</sub>: the concentration at which rate = ½ V<sub>max</sub> (her example 10 mg/L)
C<sub>p</sub> ≪ K<sub>M</sub>: twice C<sub>p</sub>, about twice the rate → first order
C<sub>p</sub> ≫ K<sub>M</sub>: rate ≈ V<sub>max</sub> → zero order

segs.text: As the dose rises into saturation, the amount removed per day still rises, but less than in proportion to the level, so the fraction removed per day falls. So the half life lengthens and the clearance falls as the dose increases. More of each dose is retained, so the A U C rises above the proportional straight line once the dose passes a certain point. Saturation can occur in absorption, distribution, metabolism or excretion, and this module deals with elimination.

card.m: into saturation: rate rises less than C<sub>p</sub> → fraction per day ↓
t<sub>½</sub> ↑, Cl ↓ as dose ↑
curve A: above the AUC ∝ dose line past a certain dose
saturable steps: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion; here: elimination

segs.text: On her log plot of level against time, curves A and B are one saturable drug at a high and a low dose, and curve C is a first order drug. B is straight like C, because at levels well below K M elimination is first order. A starts where elimination is saturated, so a smaller fraction is removed each hour and the line bends. Once A has fallen far enough it becomes straight, with the same terminal slope as B.

card.m: A: high dose; B: low dose; C: a first-order drug
B straight, like C: C<sub>p</sub> ≪ K<sub>M</sub>, first order
A: saturated at first, smaller fraction per hour → bends
terminal slopes A = B

segs.text: The same shows at steady state in her slide example. Six milligrams per kilogram per day gave a steady state level of ten milligrams per liter. A linear drug keeps the level in proportion to the dose rate, so eight would have given about thirteen. Instead, eight milligrams per kilogram per day gave twenty: one third more dose doubled the level, because elimination was saturating. She said, Small changes in dose will lead to big changes in concentration.

card.m: 6 mg/kg/day → C<sub>ss</sub> 10 mg/L
linear: 10 × {{frac:8|6}} = 13.3 mg/L
8 mg/kg/day → 20 mg/L: dose × 1.33, level × 2
small dose change → large level change

segs.text: Her written question asks the difference between linear and nonlinear pharmacokinetics, and the answer is the parameters: unchanged with dose, or changed by increased doses or chronic administration. Her signs of saturation are the half life changing with dose and the A U C out of proportion, plus two more: other drugs needing the same enzyme or carrier can change the saturation, and the ratio of the metabolites can change with dose. In her quiz the true statement was that the half life changes as the dose is increased; parameters that do not change, superposition, or an A U C in proportion describe a linear drug.

card.m: linear: parameters fixed; nonlinear: parameters change
signs: t<sub>½</sub> changes, AUC out of proportion, competing drugs, metabolite ratio changes
nonlinear: t½ changes as dose ↑; ✗ fixed parameters, superposition, AUC ∝ dose

segs.text: Her poll said a saturable drug often shows zero order at low concentrations and first order at high ones; the key is false, because it is the other way round. Low and high mean relative to K M, a concentration, never relative to V max, which is a rate. The trap is to swap the words: linear is not zero order, and nonlinear is not simply first order. The summary statement that clearance and half life are usually not constant in nonlinear processes is true. Objective two explains the order with K M and C p.

card.m: poll: zero order at low C, first order at high C? False
low or high: relative to K<sub>M</sub> (mg/L), never V<sub>max</sub> (a rate)
✗ linear = zero order; ✗ nonlinear = first order
Cl and t<sub>½</sub> usually not constant: true
